gda-sk.name: Gdańsk
gda-sk.summary: A Baltic port city in northern Poland, historically known as Danzig, a major Hanseatic trading city and later the birthplace of the Solidarity movement in the 1980s.

borscht.name: Borscht
borscht.summary: A sour soup common across Eastern and Central Europe, most often associated with a red, beetroot-based Ukrainian version, though variants without beetroot also exist.

grand-duchy-of-lithuania.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
grand-duchy-of-lithuania.summary: A sovereign state in northeastern Europe from the 13th to the late 18th century, which by 1440 stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea, the largest state in Europe.

polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.summary: A federative union of the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1569 to 1795, one of Europe's largest and most populous states, known for its elective monarchy called the Golden Liberty.

ivan-vyshenskyi.name: Ivan Vyshenskyi
ivan-vyshenskyi.summary: A Ukrainian Orthodox monk and religious philosopher (c. 1550–after 1620) considered an important polemicist of his time.

galicia-eastern-europe.name: Galicia
galicia-eastern-europe.summary: A historical region spanning southeastern Poland and western Ukraine, named after the medieval city of Halych, once part of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and later Austria's Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria.

ivan-kotliarevsky.name: Ivan Kotliarevsky
ivan-kotliarevsky.summary: Ukrainian writer and poet (1769–1838) regarded as the pioneer of modern Ukrainian literature, best known for his poem Eneida, a travesty of Virgil's Aeneid.

halu-ky.name: Halushky
halu-ky.summary: A traditional variety of thick, soft noodles or dumplings found in many Central and Eastern European cuisines.

salceson.name: Salceson
salceson.summary: A type of cooked meat product found in Polish and other Central and Eastern European cuisines, made in several varieties depending on the ingredients.

baleron.name: Baleron
baleron.summary: A Polish cured and smoked boneless pork neck cold cut, the second most valued cold cut in Poland after ham.

paul-tremo.name: Paul Tremo
paul-tremo.summary: Head chef to King Stanislaus Augustus Poniatowski of Poland, born to French Huguenots in Berlin, whose recipes helped shape modern, more cosmopolitan Polish cuisine.

stanis-aw-august-poniatowski.name: Stanisław August Poniatowski
stanis-aw-august-poniatowski.summary: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1764 to 1795, the last monarch of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, who tried to reform the ailing state.

cold-beet-soup.name: Chłodnik
cold-beet-soup.summary: A cold summer beet soup found across Belarus, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland and Ukraine, historically eaten by nobles and peasants alike in the old Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

tula-pryanik.name: Tula gingerbread
tula-pryanik.summary: A traditional Russian stamped gingerbread from the city of Tula, made from rye flour, honey and spices using hand-carved wooden molds; recorded since the 17th century.

bia-a-podlaska.name: Biała Podlaska
bia-a-podlaska.summary: A city in eastern Poland, formerly a residential seat of the Radziwiłł family, known for its palace and park ensemble and Renaissance and Baroque churches.

aristotele-fioravanti.name: Aristotele Fioravanti
aristotele-fioravanti.summary: Italian Renaissance architect and engineer (c. 1415–1486) active in Moscow from 1475, where he designed the Dormition Cathedral.

onion-dome.name: Onion dome
onion-dome.summary: Bulbous, pointed dome shape wider than its supporting drum, most associated with Russian Orthodox churches but also found across Eastern Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East.

peter-the-great.name: Peter the Great
peter-the-great.summary: Tsar of Russia from 1682 and its first emperor from 1721 until his death in 1725, who westernized Russia, built its navy, and founded St Petersburg.

elizabeth-of-russia.name: Elizabeth of Russia
elizabeth-of-russia.summary: Empress of Russia from 1741 to 1762, daughter of Peter the Great, remembered for her building projects, opposition to Prussia, and refusal to execute anyone during her reign.

russian-baroque.name: Russian Baroque
russian-baroque.summary: A Baroque artistic style in the Russian Tsardom and Empire during the late 17th and early 18th centuries, seen mainly in Saint Petersburg and Moscow under Peter the Great and Elizabeth of Russia.

naryshkin-baroque.name: Naryshkin Baroque
naryshkin-baroque.summary: A Baroque architectural style fashionable in Moscow from the late 17th to early 18th century, blending Western European Baroque with Russian tradition, named for the family whose church first used it.

yaroslavl.name: Yaroslavl
yaroslavl.summary: A Russian city on the Volga and Kotorosl rivers, part of the historic Golden Ring northeast of Moscow, with a World Heritage-listed old town.

aloisio-the-new.name: Aloisio the New
aloisio-the-new.summary: Italian Renaissance architect invited by Ivan III of Russia to work in Moscow, one of four senior Italian masters active there.

kokoshnik-architecture.name: Kokoshnik (architecture)
kokoshnik-architecture.summary: A purely decorative, semicircular or keel-shaped element on old Russian church walls, named after the headdress and especially popular in 17th-century architecture.

kazan-cathedral-moscow.name: Kazan Cathedral, Moscow
kazan-cathedral-moscow.summary: A Russian Orthodox cathedral on Red Square in Moscow; the current building is a reconstruction of the original, destroyed on Stalin's orders in 1936.

ivan-argunov.name: Ivan Argunov
ivan-argunov.summary: Russian painter and teacher (1729–1802), one of the founders of the Russian school of portrait painting.

fyodor-rokotov.name: Fyodor Rokotov
fyodor-rokotov.summary: A Russian portrait painter (1736–1808) born a peasant serf who bought his freedom and became one of the finest portraitists of his time, known for psychological, understated depictions.

dmitry-levitzky.name: Dmitry Levitzky
dmitry-levitzky.summary: Ukrainian-born Russian portrait painter and academician (1735–1822).

vladimir-borovikovsky.name: Vladimir Borovikovsky
vladimir-borovikovsky.summary: Russian artist of Ukrainian Cossack origin (1757–1825) who served at Catherine the Great's court and dominated Russian portrait painting around 1800.

imperial-academy-of-arts.name: Russian Academy of Arts
imperial-academy-of-arts.summary: An art academy in Saint Petersburg founded in 1757, later renamed the Imperial Academy of Arts by Catherine the Great, which promoted neoclassical style and trained Russia's leading artists.

tienne-maurice-falconet.name: Étienne Maurice Falconet
tienne-maurice-falconet.summary: French sculptor (1716–1791) best known for the Bronze Horseman, an equestrian statue of Peter the Great in Saint Petersburg.

catherine-the-great.name: Catherine the Great
catherine-the-great.summary: Empress of Russia from 1762 to 1796, who seized power from her husband Peter III and oversaw an era of territorial expansion and Enlightenment reform.

pietro-antonio-solari.name: Pietro Antonio Solari
pietro-antonio-solari.summary: Italian Renaissance architect and sculptor (c. 1445–1493) invited to Moscow by Ivan III to help rebuild the Kremlin's walls and towers.

novodevichy-convent.name: Novodevichy Convent
novodevichy-convent.summary: A Moscow convent founded in 1524 by Grand Duke Vasily III to mark the capture of Smolensk, largely unchanged since the 17th century and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

donskoy-monastery.name: Donskoy Monastery
donskoy-monastery.summary: A major Moscow monastery founded in 1591 to commemorate the city's deliverance from a threatened Crimean Khan invasion, guarding the southern approach to the Kremlin.

nizhny-novgorod.name: Nizhny Novgorod
nizhny-novgorod.summary: A Russian city founded in 1221 at the meeting of the Oka and Volga rivers, a major trade centre from 1817 and later, as Gorky, an important Soviet industrial city.

solvychegodsk.name: Solvychegodsk
solvychegodsk.summary: A small town in Arkhangelsk Oblast, Russia, on the Vychegda River, with a 2010 population of about 2,460.

ustyuzhna.name: Ustyuzhna
ustyuzhna.summary: A Russian town on the Mologa River in Vologda Oblast, home to the Church of Our Lady of Kazan, built in the Stroganov Baroque style.

pustozersk.name: Pustozersk
pustozersk.summary: The first Russian town built north of the Arctic Circle, founded in 1499 on the Pechora River as a military outpost, later used as a place of exile.

samoyedic-peoples.name: Samoyedic peoples
samoyedic-peoples.summary: A group of related peoples speaking Uralic languages, indigenous to parts of Siberia.

pechora-river.name: Pechora River
pechora-river.summary: The sixth-longest river in Europe, flowing from northwest Russia into the Arctic Ocean, mostly through the Komi Republic.

crimean-khanate.name: Crimean Khanate
crimean-khanate.summary: A Crimean Tatar state founded by Hacı I Giray in 1441 that at its height stretched from Bessarabia to the North Caucasus, before being annexed by Russia in 1783.

tsardom-of-russia.name: Tsardom of Russia
tsardom-of-russia.summary: Centralized Russian state from 1547, when Ivan IV took the title of tsar, until 1721, when Peter the Great proclaimed the Russian Empire.

time-of-troubles.name: Time of Troubles
time-of-troubles.summary: A period of political crisis in Russia, 1598 to 1613, marked by famine, false claimants to the throne, and foreign occupation, ending with the rise of the Romanovs.

battle-of-klushino.name: Battle of Klushino
battle-of-klushino.summary: 1610 battle in which an outnumbered Polish-Lithuanian force decisively beat Russia's army, remembered as one of the greatest triumphs of Polish cavalry.

selim-ii.name: Selim II
selim-ii.summary: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1566 to 1574, nicknamed Selim the Blond or the Drunkard, whose reign saw the conquest of Cyprus and Tunis but defeat at the Battle of Lepanto.

astrakhan.name: Astrakhan
astrakhan.summary: A city on the Volga in southern Russia, formerly capital of the Khanate of Astrakhan, captured by Ivan the Terrible in 1556.

battle-of-poltava.name: Battle of Poltava
battle-of-poltava.summary: The decisive 8 July 1709 battle of the Great Northern War, in which Russia's Peter I defeated Sweden's Charles XII, ending Sweden's status as a European great power and marking the rise of Russian dominance in eastern Europe.

russian-conquest-of-siberia.name: Russian conquest of Siberia
russian-conquest-of-siberia.summary: Russia's takeover of Siberia between 1581 and 1778, beginning with Yermak Timofeyevich's campaign against the Siberian Khanate and marked by fierce fighting with indigenous peoples.

charles-xii-of-sweden.name: Charles XII of Sweden
charles-xii-of-sweden.summary: King of Sweden from 1697 to 1718 who led Swedish forces to repeated victories against a much larger coalition in the Great Northern War, including at Narva in 1700.

seven-boyars.name: Seven Boyars
seven-boyars.summary: A group of seven Russian nobles who deposed Tsar Vasili Shuisky in July 1610 and, after a military defeat, agreed to Polish-Lithuanian occupation of Moscow.

w-adys-aw-iv-vasa.name: Władysław IV Vasa
w-adys-aw-iv-vasa.summary: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1595-1648) who, as a young prince, was briefly elected tsar of Russia in 1610 but never took the throne.

sigismund-iii-vasa.name: Sigismund III Vasa
sigismund-iii-vasa.summary: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1587 to 1632, and King of Sweden from 1592 to 1599, who imposed Catholicism and expanded Poland's territory before being deposed in Sweden.

ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.name: Ibrahim Pasha
ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.summary: An Egyptian general and the eldest son of Muhammad Ali, who commanded Egyptian and Ottoman armies and briefly ruled Egypt and Sudan as regent before dying only four months later, in 1848.

chyhyryn.name: Chyhyryn
chyhyryn.summary: A city in central Ukraine that served as the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate from 1648 to 1669.

selim-i-giray.name: Selim I Giray
selim-i-giray.summary: Khan of the Crimean Khanate four separate times between 1671 and 1704, repeatedly appointed and removed by the Ottomans, and regarded as an unusually capable ruler with no conflicts with his nobles.

ivan-mazepa.name: Ivan Mazepa
ivan-mazepa.summary: Hetman of the Cossack Hetmanate from 1687 to 1709 who abandoned his alliance with Tsar Peter I to side with Charles XII of Sweden, going into exile after their defeat at Poltava.

great-frost-of-1709.name: Great Frost of 1709
great-frost-of-1709.summary: An extraordinarily cold winter across Europe in 1708 to 1709, known as 'Le Grand Hiver' in France and the coldest European winter in the past 500 years.

cossack-hetmanate.name: Cossack Hetmanate
cossack-hetmanate.summary: A Cossack state in what is now central Ukraine, existing from 1648 to 1764, first recognized under the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth before coming under Russian suzerainty.

bohdan-khmelnytsky.name: Bohdan Khmelnytsky
bohdan-khmelnytsky.summary: Cossack military commander (c. 1595–1657) who led an uprising against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and allied the new Cossack state with Russia in 1654.

pereiaslav-agreement.name: Treaty of Pereiaslav
pereiaslav-agreement.summary: A 1654 pact in which Cossack leader Bohdan Khmelnytsky pledged allegiance to the Russian tsar, placing the Cossack Hetmanate under Russian protection.

battle-of-molodi.name: Battle of Molodi
battle-of-molodi.summary: A July-August 1572 battle near Moscow in which Russian and Cossack forces under Prince Mikhail Vorotynsky decisively defeated the Crimean Khanate, which had burned Moscow the year before.

ivan-samoylovych.name: Ivan Samoylovych
ivan-samoylovych.summary: Hetman of Left-bank Ukraine from 1672 to 1687, whose rule saw the Cossack Hetmanate further absorbed into the Tsardom of Russia.

grigory-romodanovsky.name: Grigory Romodanovsky
grigory-romodanovsky.summary: A controversial Russian general who helped bring Ukrainian Cossack officers under Muscovite rule and led Tsar Alexis's forces in Ukraine during the Russo-Polish War.

sula-dnieper.name: Sula
sula-dnieper.summary: Left tributary of the Dnieper River in Ukraine, 363 kilometres long, forming a large delta with numerous islands where the two rivers meet.

q-r-m-giray.name: Qırım Giray
q-r-m-giray.summary: Khan Qırım Giray (1717–1769), remembered as one of the most influential rulers of the Crimean Khanate and as patron of the Bakhchisaray Fountain and many Crimean mosques.

fortress-of-st-elizabeth.name: Fortress of St. Elizabeth
fortress-of-st-elizabeth.summary: A six-pointed star-shaped earthen fortress in what is now Kropyvnytskyi, central Ukraine, and the city's main symbol.

ivan-fyodorov-printer.name: Ivan Fedorov
ivan-fyodorov-printer.summary: One of the fathers of Eastern Slavonic printing, also a skilled cannon maker, who was forced out of Moscow over his printing techniques and, in exile in Poland–Lithuania, was instrumental in publishing the Ostrog Bible; he died in 1583.

alexander-radishchev.name: Alexander Radishchev
alexander-radishchev.summary: A Russian author and social critic (1749–1802) exiled to Siberia by Catherine the Great for his 1790 work exposing Russia's social conditions.

ostroh.name: Ostroh
ostroh.summary: A city on the Horyn River in western Ukraine, home to the country's first higher-education institution (1576) and to early printed East Slavic books like the Ostrog Bible.

konstanty-wasyl-ostrogski.name: Vasyl-Kostiantyn Ostrozky
konstanty-wasyl-ostrogski.summary: Kostiantyn-Vasyl Ostrozky: Powerful Ruthenian Orthodox magnate of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (1526–1608), founder of the Ostroh Academy and protector of Eastern Orthodoxy.

ostrog-bible.name: Ostrog Bible
ostrog-bible.summary: The first complete printed Bible in Church Slavonic, produced in Ostrog in 1581 by the printer Ivan Fyodorov under a local prince's patronage.

church-slavonic.name: Church Slavonic
church-slavonic.summary: A South Slavic liturgical language descended from 9th- to 10th-century Old Church Slavonic, still used today in Eastern Orthodox worship across many Slavic countries.

ivan-franko.name: Ivan Franko
ivan-franko.summary: Ukrainian poet, writer and political activist (1856–1916) who founded Western Ukraine's socialist-nationalist movement and translated many major European writers into Ukrainian.

yelysei-pletenetskyi.name: Yelisey Pletenetsky
yelysei-pletenetskyi.summary: A Ukrainian archimandrite (1550-1624) of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth who led the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra monastery from 1599 until his death.

kyiv-pechersk-lavra.name: Kyiv Pechersk Lavra
kyiv-pechersk-lavra.summary: A historic Eastern Christian monastery founded as a cave monastery in Kyiv in the 11th century, long a leading religious center in Eastern Europe and an early printing hub in Ukraine.

book-of-hours.name: Book of Hours
book-of-hours.summary: A Christian prayer book used to pray the canonical hours, especially popular in the Middle Ages and the most common surviving type of medieval illuminated manuscript.

pochaiv-lavra.name: Pochaiv Lavra
pochaiv-lavra.summary: A monastery and lavra in western Ukraine that has been a major center of Eastern Orthodoxy, and later Greek Catholicism, since medieval times.

chernihiv.name: Chernihiv
chernihiv.summary: A city in northern Ukraine that was the Rus' state's second most important city after Kyiv in the 9th century, and later a major cultural center under the Cossack Hetmanate.

meletius-smotrytsky.name: Meletius Smotrytsky
meletius-smotrytsky.summary: A Ruthenian writer, linguist and Archbishop of Polotsk (c. 1577–1633) whose 1619 Slavonic Grammar became the standard grammar book in Russia until the late 18th century.

ippolit-bogdanovich.name: Ippolit Bogdanovich
ippolit-bogdanovich.summary: Russian classicist and rococo poet (1744–1803), best known for his long poem Dushenka (1778).

giles-fletcher-the-elder.name: Giles Fletcher, the Elder
giles-fletcher-the-elder.summary: English poet and diplomat (c. 1548–1611) and member of Parliament, best known for the sonnet sequence Licia; father of poet Giles Fletcher, the Younger.

samuel-collins-physician-born-1619.name: Samuel Collins
samuel-collins-physician-born-1619.summary: An English physician who served as personal doctor to Tsar Alexis I of Russia from 1659 to 1666 and wrote The Present State of Russia (1671).

omeljan-pritsak.name: Omeljan Pritsak
omeljan-pritsak.summary: Ukrainian-American historian (1919–2006) who became Harvard's first Mykhailo Hrushevsky Professor of Ukrainian History and founded its Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute.

harvard-library-of-early-ukrainian-liter.name: Harvard Library of Early Ukrainian Literature
harvard-library-of-early-ukrainian-liter.summary: A publication series launched by Omeljan Pritsak in 1987 to make major Ukrainian literary works from the 11th to 18th centuries available, funded by the Ukrainian diaspora in North America.
harvard-library-of-early-ukrainian-liter.source_title: Harvard Library of Early Ukrainian Literature

vasily-lyovshin.name: Vasily Lyovshin
vasily-lyovshin.summary: A Russian writer (1746–1826) who wrote on agricultural and economic subjects and moved in Nikolay Novikov's circle; his 1784 utopian novel contains the first Russian fictional flight to the Moon.

russian-academy-of-sciences.name: Russian Academy of Sciences
russian-academy-of-sciences.summary: Russia's national academy of sciences, established by Peter the Great in 1724 as the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences with guidance from Gottfried Leibniz, now headquartered in Moscow.

gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz.summary: A German polymath (1646–1716) credited alongside Isaac Newton with inventing calculus, and a major figure in the history of philosophy and mathematics, called the 'last universal genius'.

leonhard-euler.name: Leonhard Euler
leonhard-euler.summary: A Swiss mathematician and polymath (1707–1783) who founded graph theory and topology, advanced many branches of mathematics and physics, and introduced much modern mathematical notation while working in Saint Petersburg and Berlin.

daniel-bernoulli.name: Daniel Bernoulli
daniel-bernoulli.summary: Swiss mathematician and physicist (1700–1782) of the Bernoulli family, known for Bernoulli's principle in fluid mechanics, underlying the carburetor and the aeroplane wing.

christian-goldbach.name: Christian Goldbach
christian-goldbach.summary: Prussian mathematician (1690–1764) known for number theory and Goldbach's conjecture, who also worked in Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and was a close friend of Leonhard Euler.

great-northern-expedition.name: Second Kamchatka Expedition
great-northern-expedition.summary: A Russian Arctic expedition of roughly 1733 to 1743, led by Vitus Bering, that mapped most of Siberia's Arctic coast and much of Arctic North America, involving over 3,000 people.

vitus-bering.name: Vitus Bering
vitus-bering.summary: Danish-born Russian cartographer, explorer and naval officer (1681–1741) who led two expeditions charting northeastern Asia and the western coast of North America; the Bering Strait and Sea are named after him.

peter-simon-pallas.name: Peter Simon Pallas
peter-simon-pallas.summary: Prussian naturalist and explorer (1741–1811) who worked in the Russian Empire between 1767 and 1810, studying its zoology, botany and geography.

transit-of-venus.name: Transit of Venus
transit-of-venus.summary: A rare astronomical event in which Venus passes across the face of the Sun, historically used to calculate the distance from Earth to Venus and the scale of the solar system.

saint-petersburg-state-university.name: Saint Petersburg State University
saint-petersburg-state-university.summary: Public research university in Saint Petersburg founded in 1724 by decree of Peter the Great, one of Russia's oldest, with a focus on fundamental science and engineering research.

mikhail-lomonosov.name: Mikhail Lomonosov
mikhail-lomonosov.summary: Russian polymath, scientist and writer (1711–1765) who discovered the atmosphere of Venus and the law of conservation of mass, predicted Antarctica's existence, and helped shape modern Russian literary language.

moscow-state-university.name: Moscow State University
moscow-state-university.summary: A public research university in Moscow whose alumni include past Soviet leaders and multiple Nobel, Fields Medal and Turing Award winners.

christian-wolff-philosopher.name: Christian Wolff
christian-wolff-philosopher.summary: German philosopher (1679–1754) ranked among the most eminent between Leibniz and Kant, and a founding figure of economics and public administration as academic disciplines.

caspar-friedrich-wolff.name: Caspar Friedrich Wolff
caspar-friedrich-wolff.summary: German physiologist and embryologist (1733–1794) regarded as one of the pioneers of modern embryology.

joseph-nicolas-delisle.name: Joseph-Nicolas Delisle
joseph-nicolas-delisle.summary: French astronomer and cartographer (1688–1768) best known for inventing the Delisle temperature scale in 1732.

nevil-maskelyne.name: Nevil Maskelyne
nevil-maskelyne.summary: Britain's fifth Astronomer Royal (1765-1811), the first to scientifically measure Earth's mass and creator of The Nautical Almanac.

nicolaus-ii-bernoulli.name: Nicolaus II Bernoulli
nicolaus-ii-bernoulli.summary: Swiss mathematician (1695–1726) from the prominent Bernoulli family, son of Johann Bernoulli and brother of Daniel Bernoulli, who died in Saint Petersburg.

ivan-the-terrible.name: Ivan IV
ivan-the-terrible.summary: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1533 and Russia's first Tsar from 1547 until his death in 1584, known as Ivan the Terrible; his reign turned Russia into an empire at great cost to its people.

great-northern-war.name: Great Northern War
great-northern-war.summary: A war from 1700 to 1721 in which a coalition led by Russia broke Sweden's dominance over Northern, Central and Eastern Europe, ending with Russia as the region's leading power.

boyar.name: Boyar
boyar.summary: A member of the highest-ranking feudal nobility in medieval Eastern European states such as Kievan Rus', Bulgaria, Moldavia and Wallachia, ranking just below princes and tsars.

polish-russian-war-1654-1667.name: Russo-Polish War (1654–1667)
polish-russian-war-1654-1667.summary: A war between the Tsardom of Russia and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, overlapping with the Swedish invasion known as 'The Deluge'; it ended with a Russian-favoring truce and marked Russia's rise as a great power.

truce-of-andrusovo.name: Truce of Andrusovo
truce-of-andrusovo.summary: A thirteen-and-a-half-year truce signed in 1667 between the Tsardom of Russia and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, ending the Russo-Polish War that had begun in 1654.

pale-of-settlement.name: Pale of Settlement
pale-of-settlement.summary: A western region of the Russian Empire, existing from 1791 to 1917, where Jewish residents were mostly required to live, established under Catherine the Great after Russia's partition of Poland.

shtetl.name: Shtetl
shtetl.summary: A Yiddish term for small towns with large Ashkenazi Jewish populations in Eastern Europe before the Holocaust, mainly found in the 19th-century Russian Pale of Settlement and neighboring regions.

governing-senate.name: Governing Senate
governing-senate.summary: The highest legislative, judicial and executive body under the Russian emperors from 1711 to 1917, instituted by Peter the Great to replace the Boyar Duma.

table-of-ranks.name: Table of Ranks
table-of-ranks.summary: A formal list of military, government and court positions in Imperial Russia, introduced by Peter the Great in 1722 and abolished in 1917.

treaty-of-nystad.name: Treaty of Nystad
treaty-of-nystad.summary: 1721 treaty ending the Great Northern War between Russia and Sweden, transferring Estonia, Livonia and Ingria to Russia.

karelia.name: Karelia
karelia.summary: A cultural region of Northern Europe divided between northwestern Russia and Finland, historically significant to Russia, Finland and Sweden.

ingria.name: Ingria
ingria.summary: A historical region in northwestern Russia along the Gulf of Finland, originally home to Finnic peoples, later passed from Sweden to Russia and briefly independent from 1919 to 1920.

livonia.name: Livonia
livonia.summary: A historical region on present-day Latvia and Estonia, named after the Livonians, conquered during the Livonian Crusade of 1193-1290.

heraclius-ii-of-georgia.name: Heraclius II
heraclius-ii-of-georgia.summary: King of Kakheti from 1744 and of the united Kartli-Kakheti from 1762 to 1798, in eastern Georgia; he unified the region and placed it under Russian protection in 1783.

treaty-of-georgievsk.name: Treaty of Georgievsk
treaty-of-georgievsk.summary: A 1783 treaty making eastern Georgia a Russian protectorate under the Bagrationi dynasty; Russia later scrapped it in 1801, annexing Georgian lands directly and deposing the monarchy.

agha-mohammad-khan-qajar.name: Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar
agha-mohammad-khan-qajar.summary: Founder of Iran's Qajar dynasty, ruling as Shah from 1789 to 1797; he reunified the country, made Tehran its capital, and campaigned to reassert Iranian rule over Georgia.

zaporozhian-sich.name: Zaporozhian Sich
zaporozhian-sich.summary: A semi-autonomous Cossack polity on the lower Dnieper River active from the 16th to 18th centuries, dissolved by Catherine the Great in 1775.

novorossiya-governorate.name: Novorossiya Governorate
novorossiya-governorate.summary: An administrative region of the Russian Empire existing 1764–1783 and 1796–1802, established after Russia gained access to the Black Sea and founded cities such as Kherson and Odessa.

kherson.name: Kherson
kherson.summary: A port city in southern Ukraine on the Black Sea and Dnieper River, founded by the Russian Empire as a fleet base on a former Cossack fortress site, later known for shipbuilding and watermelons.

polish-russian-peace-treaty-1686.name: Treaty of Perpetual Peace
polish-russian-peace-treaty-1686.summary: A 1686 peace treaty between Russia and Poland-Lithuania ending the Russo-Polish War of 1654 to 1667; it confirmed the earlier Truce of Andrusovo and brought Russia into an anti-Ottoman alliance with Poland, the Holy Roman Empire and Venice.

sejm.name: Sejm
sejm.summary: The historic parliament of the Kingdom of Poland, strengthened by the 1573 Henrician Articles into a constitutional elective monarchy; the term now names the lower house of Poland's parliament.

theophan-prokopovich.name: Feofan Prokopovich
theophan-prokopovich.summary: A Russian Orthodox bishop, theologian, and scholar of Ukrainian origin (1681–1736) who implemented Peter the Great's church reforms and led the Most Holy Synod from 1722.

stefan-yavorsky.name: Stefan Yavorsky
stefan-yavorsky.summary: An archbishop and statesman in the Russian Empire (1658–1722) who became the first president of the Most Holy Synod.

hryhorii-skovoroda.name: Grigory Skovoroda
hryhorii-skovoroda.summary: A Ukrainian Cossack-born philosopher, poet, teacher and composer (1722–1794) who lived in the Russian Empire and was often called a 'Socrates' for his way of life.

martinism.name: Martinism
martinism.summary: A form of Christian mysticism concerned with humanity's fall from a divine source and its eventual "Reintegration," first transmitted through a Masonic system founded around 1740 in France.

patriarch-nikon-of-moscow.name: Patriarch Nikon
patriarch-nikon-of-moscow.summary: The seventh Patriarch of Moscow (served 1652-1666), close to Tsar Alexis, whose liturgical reforms caused the lasting schism (Raskol) in the Russian Orthodox Church.

old-believers.name: Old Believers
old-believers.summary: Followers of the pre-1650s Russian Orthodox liturgy who split from the Church after Patriarch Nikon's reforms, often fleeing persecution and preserving traditional Russian customs like long beards.

schism-of-the-russian-church.name: Raskol
schism-of-the-russian-church.summary: Russian term for the schism of the 1660s to 1690s sparked by Patriarch Nikon's church reforms, which split off dissenting Old Believers and led to persecution by church and state.

spiritual-christianity.name: Spiritual Christianity
spiritual-christianity.summary: A group of heterodox Russian Christian movements that arose from imported Protestant influences and dissatisfaction with Orthodox clergy, including sects like the Doukhobors.

union-of-brest.name: Union of Brest
union-of-brest.summary: An agreement in 1595–96 by Eastern Orthodox churches in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth to accept papal authority while keeping Orthodox rites, creating the Ruthenian Uniate Church, ancestor of today's Ukrainian and Belarusian Greek Catholic Churches.

ukrainian-greek-catholic-church.name: Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
ukrainian-greek-catholic-church.summary: An Eastern Catholic church based in Ukraine, in full communion with Rome, tracing itself to the 1596 Union of Brest that shifted Ruthenian Orthodox believers to the Holy See's jurisdiction.

vasily-tatishchev.name: Vasily Tatishchev
vasily-tatishchev.summary: A Russian statesman, historian, philosopher and ethnographer (1686–1750) who wrote a posthumously published history of Russia and founded the cities of Stavropol-on-Volga, Yekaterinburg and Perm.

andrey-bolotov.name: Andrey Bolotov
andrey-bolotov.summary: The most prolific memoirist and most distinguished agriculturist of 18th-century Russia (1738–1833), known for pioneering work in crop rotation and plant breeding.

alexis-of-russia.name: Alexei Mikhailovich
alexis-of-russia.summary: Tsar of all Russia from 1645 to 1676, the second Romanov tsar, who was the first to sign laws on his own authority and oversaw wars with Iran, Poland and Sweden.

hasidic-judaism.name: Hasidic Judaism
hasidic-judaism.summary: A religious revival movement within Judaism that arose in 18th-century Western Ukraine, founded by Israel Ben Eliezer (the "Baal Shem Tov"), known for its conservatism and hereditary Rebbe leaders.

jakob-b-hme.name: Jakob Böhme
jakob-b-hme.summary: German philosopher, Christian mystic and Lutheran theologian (1575–1624) whose scandalous first book later deeply influenced German idealism and Romanticism.

gnosticism.name: Gnosticism
gnosticism.summary: A collection of religious and philosophical ideas that developed among early Christian sects by the mid-second century, valuing personal spiritual knowledge over church authority.

metropolis-of-kyiv.name: Metropolis of Kyiv
metropolis-of-kyiv.summary: An autonomous church body under the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, formed in Kyiv in 988 after the Christianization of Rus, whose jurisdiction later passed through Rome and then Moscow.

ecumenical-patriarch-of-constantinople.name: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople
ecumenical-patriarch-of-constantinople.summary: The archbishop of Constantinople and spiritual leader of Eastern Orthodox Christians worldwide, regarded as first among equals among Orthodox church heads.

dionysius-iv-of-constantinople.name: Dionysius IV of Constantinople
dionysius-iv-of-constantinople.summary: Served as Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople five separate times between 1671 and 1694, before his death in 1696.

little-russia.name: Little Russia
little-russia.summary: A historical and geographic term for Ukraine, first distinguishing 'Great' and 'Little' Rus' church jurisdictions in the 14th century before later denoting most of modern Ukraine.

great-russia.name: Great Russia
great-russia.summary: A historical name for the Russian heartland centered on the Grand Duchy of Moscow and later the Tsardom of Russia, distinguished in official Tsarist titles from 1654 from Little Russia and White Russia.

podolia.name: Podolia
podolia.summary: A historic region of fertile farmland in west-central and southwestern Ukraine, ruled over time by Galicia-Volhynia, the Golden Horde, Poland-Lithuania, the Ottomans and Russia.

bolokhovians.name: Bolokhovians
bolokhovians.summary: A 13th-century Slavic ethnic group near Galicia, Volhynia and Kiev, whose princes often clashed with Daniel of Galicia–Volhynia and vanished after his 1257 victory.

zbruch-idol.name: Zbruch Idol
zbruch-idol.summary: A 9th-century limestone pillar, one of the few surviving monuments of pre-Christian Slavic belief, long linked to the deity Svetovit though some scholars suspect it is a 19th-century fake.

svetovit.name: Svetovid
svetovit.summary: God of abundance and war and chief deity of the Slavic Rani tribe and Polabian Slavs, worshipped at a temple on the island of Rügen until it was destroyed in 1168.

kokoshnik.name: Kokoshnik
kokoshnik.summary: A traditional Russian women's headdress worn with the sarafan, dating to 10th-century Novgorod and especially popular in northern Russia from the 16th to 19th centuries.

bast-shoe.name: Bast shoes (lapti)
bast-shoe.summary: Traditional woven shoes made from tree-bark fibre, worn by poorer people in the forested regions of Northeastern Europe including Russians, Balts and Scandinavians; easy to make but not durable.

ushanka.name: Ushanka
ushanka.summary: A Russian fur hat with ear flaps that can be tied up or fastened under the chin for warmth, traditionally worn across Eastern Europe and the Baltic region.

valenki.name: Valenki
valenki.summary: Traditional Russian felt winter boots without outer soles, regarded as national footwear and still worn especially in Siberia.
